name: Deltoid
func: The rounded muscle that caps the shoulder. It lifts the arm out to the side, and its front and back parts swing the arm forward and backward.

levels.kid:
Touch the round top of your shoulder. That bump is a muscle called the **deltoid**.

It is shaped like a **triangle** pointing down your arm. When you lift your arm out to the side, like a bird flapping its wings, your deltoid is doing the work. The front part helps you reach forward, and the back part helps you swing your arm back.

It also makes your shoulder look round and covers the top of your shoulder joint like a cushion. Doctors and nurses often give shots into this muscle!
levels.hs:
The **deltoid** is the thick, triangular muscle that forms the rounded contour of the shoulder. Its name comes from the Greek letter delta (Δ). It wraps over the front, side and back of the **shoulder (glenohumeral) joint**, lying just under the skin and over the rotator cuff tendons.

It has three parts. **Anterior fibres** start on the outer third of the **clavicle**. **Middle fibres** start on the **acromion** (the top bony point of the shoulder). **Posterior fibres** start on the **spine of the scapula**. All three converge to insert on the **deltoid tuberosity**, a rough bump halfway down the outer side of the **humerus**.

Together the fibres **abduct** the arm (raise it to the side). The anterior part also flexes and medially rotates the arm (reaching forward), and the posterior part extends and laterally rotates it (pulling back).

The deltoid is supplied by the **axillary nerve**, from spinal roots C5 and C6. Next to it, the **pectoralis major** lies in front, separated by a groove carrying the **cephalic vein**.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** origin from the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, mirroring the insertion of trapezius; insertion on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.

**Innervation and blood supply:** the **axillary nerve (C5–C6)** leaves the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, passes through the **quadrangular space** (bounded by teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the surgical neck of the humerus) with the **posterior circumflex humeral artery**, and winds around the **surgical neck** to reach the deep surface of the muscle. It also supplies teres minor and gives the **superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm** to the skin over the lower deltoid (the "regimental badge" area). Blood comes mainly from the posterior circumflex humeral and thoraco-acromial arteries.

**Function:** abduction is shared with **supraspinatus**. The common teaching is that supraspinatus starts abduction (first ~15°) and the deltoid continues, but EMG shows both are active from the start; supraspinatus mainly stabilises the humeral head early, when the deltoid's pull is largely upward. Above about 90°, scapular rotation by **trapezius** and **serratus anterior** is required to raise the arm fully overhead (**scapulohumeral rhythm**).

**Relations:** the **subacromial-subdeltoid bursa** lies deep to the deltoid, separating it from the rotator cuff. The **deltopectoral groove** between the anterior deltoid and pectoralis major carries the cephalic vein and is a landmark for surgical approaches.
levels.phd:
The deltoid's middle part is **multipennate**: several internal tendinous septa give it many short, obliquely arranged fascicles. This architecture increases **physiological cross-sectional area** at the cost of excursion, so the middle deltoid is built for force, while the more parallel-fibred anterior and posterior parts allow greater shortening and speed. Some anatomists describe up to seven functional segments based on innervation and fibre direction.

Its mechanical action changes with arm position. At the side, the line of action of the middle deltoid is nearly parallel to the humerus, producing **shear** that drives the humeral head upward against the acromion. The rotator cuff provides a compressive **force couple** that centres the head in the glenoid, letting the deltoid's torque generate rotation instead of translation. This is why a massive rotator cuff tear can cause superior migration of the head.

Motor unit studies show regional recruitment depending on direction of force, supporting the idea that the CNS controls the deltoid as multiple compartments. Axillary nerve branches split early into anterior and posterior divisions, with the posterior branch also supplying teres minor and the cutaneous branch.

Muscle fibre type composition is mixed, roughly half **type I** (slow oxidative) in most sampled adults, suiting both postural holding and fast movements. The deltoid is a common biopsy site in research on muscle adaptation and myopathy because it is accessible and frequently involved in proximal muscle diseases.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect for wasting (a flattened, "squared-off" shoulder with a prominent acromion) and test abduction strength from 15–90°. Check sensation over the **regimental badge area** on the upper lateral arm.

**Axillary nerve injury** occurs with **anterior shoulder dislocation** and **surgical neck of humerus fractures**. It gives weak abduction, deltoid wasting and numbness of the badge area. Always test and document axillary nerve function before and after reducing a dislocation. Most traction injuries recover; persistent cases are investigated with EMG and may need nerve grafting or transfer (for example, a branch of the radial nerve to triceps transferred to the axillary nerve).

**Distinguishing weak abduction:** C5 radiculopathy (weak deltoid and biceps, reduced biceps reflex, neck pain), upper trunk brachial plexus injury (**Erb's palsy**, "waiter's tip" posture), rotator cuff tear (painful arc, weak external rotation, normal deltoid bulk early), and **Parsonage–Turner syndrome** (sudden severe shoulder pain followed by weakness).

The deltoid is a favoured site for **intramuscular injections**, including many vaccines; the safe zone is the thick central part about 2–3 finger widths below the acromion, avoiding the axillary nerve lower down and the bursa above. Injections placed too high can inflame the subacromial bursa.

In **reverse total shoulder arthroplasty**, used for cuff-deficient shoulders, the joint's centre of rotation is moved medially and downward so the deltoid alone can raise the arm. Deltoid function is therefore essential before this surgery. In proximal muscle diseases (myositis, muscular dystrophies), deltoid weakness is an early finding.

keyPoints: Origin clavicle, acromion and scapular spine; insertion deltoid tuberosity
Main abductor of the arm (with supraspinatus)
Axillary nerve C5–C6 through the quadrangular space
Shoulder dislocation can injure the axillary nerve → badge-area numbness

test.explain: The axillary nerve (C5–C6) winds around the surgical neck of the humerus to reach the deltoid.

test.q: The deltoid inserts on the deltoid ______ of the humerus.
test.explain: All three parts converge on this bump on the lateral shaft.

test.q: After an anterior shoulder dislocation, numbness over the upper outer arm suggests injury to which nerve?
test.explain: The superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm comes from the axillary nerve (regimental badge area).

test.q: Which part of the deltoid is multipennate and built for force?
test.explain: Multipennate fibres increase cross-sectional area, giving the middle deltoid its strength.

test.q: The vein running in the groove between deltoid and pectoralis major is the ______ vein.
test.explain: The deltopectoral groove carries the cephalic vein to the axillary vein.
